statement: For a [simplicial set](c:simplicial-set) $K$, integration over simplices is a natural [quasi-isomorphism](c:quasi-isomorphism) $\int\colon A_{PL}(K)\to C^*(K;\mathbb{Q})$ from the [polynomial differential forms](c:polynomial-differential-form) on $K$ to the rational simplicial cochains.

hypotheses.text: $K$ is a [simplicial set](c:simplicial-set), for example the simplicial set of a [simplicial complex](c:simplicial-complex).
The coefficient field is $\mathbb{Q}$, so every nonzero integer is invertible.

conclusion: The map $\int$ induces an isomorphism $H^*(A_{PL}(K))\cong H^*(K;\mathbb{Q})$ of [cohomology](c:cohomology), natural in $K$.

proofs.name: Skeletal induction
proofs.slogan: Compare forms and cochains skeleton by skeleton, using the Poincaré lemma on each simplex, then pass to the limit.
proofs.scope: The additive statement for every simplicial set, with no finiteness condition. The multiplicative refinement (the induced isomorphism respects products) is cited from Bousfield and Gugenheim and is not proved here.

roles.why: Characteristic zero lets the Poincaré lemma divide by $k+1$ when it integrates $t^k\,dt$.
The skeleta and the nondegenerate simplices of $K$ organize the induction and the limit.

steps.slogan: Prove the Poincaré lemma for polynomial forms on the standard simplex.
steps.detail: $A_{PL}(\Delta^n)$ is $\mathbb{Q}[t_1,\dots,t_n]\otimes\Lambda(dt_1,\dots,dt_n)$, a tensor product of $n$ copies of $\mathbb{Q}[t]\otimes\Lambda(dt)$. In one variable, $t^k\,dt=d\bigl(t^{k+1}/(k+1)\bigr)$ makes every form of positive degree exact. The Künneth formula gives cohomology $\mathbb{Q}$ in degree $0$ only.

steps.slogan: Define integration over simplices and show that it is a natural cochain map.
steps.detail: For $\omega\in A^p_{PL}(K)$ and a $p$-simplex $\sigma$, set $(\int\omega)(\sigma)=\int_{\Delta^p}\sigma^*\omega$, a rational number. Stokes' theorem on $\Delta^p$ gives $\int d\omega=\pm\,\delta\int\omega$. Compatibility with faces and degeneracies makes $\int$ natural in $K$.

steps.slogan: Show that restriction of forms from a simplex to its boundary is onto.
steps.detail: A form on $\partial\Delta^n$ is a compatible family of forms on the facets. Extend it facet by facet: a form on a facet that vanishes on the earlier facets lies in the product of the ideals $(t_i,dt_i)$, so it extends by the same product. So restriction from $\operatorname{sk}_nK$ to $\operatorname{sk}_{n-1}K$ is onto, with kernel $\prod A_{PL}(\Delta^n,\partial\Delta^n)$.

steps.slogan: Show that integration is a quasi-isomorphism on each simplex pair.
steps.detail: Compare the long [exact sequences](c:exact-sequence) of $(\Delta^n,\partial\Delta^n)$ for forms and for cochains. The $\Delta^n$ terms are acyclic with $\int$ an isomorphism on $H^0$, by step 1. The $\partial\Delta^n$ terms agree by induction on the dimension. The five lemma then gives the relative terms, which have cohomology only in degree $n$.

steps.slogan: Glue the simplices onto the skeleton and compare the two long exact sequences.
steps.detail: The short exact sequences for $\operatorname{sk}_nK\to\operatorname{sk}_{n-1}K$ exist for forms by step 3 and for cochains by definition. Integration maps one to the other. The relative terms agree by step 4 and $\operatorname{sk}_{n-1}K$ agrees by induction, so the five lemma shows that $\int$ is a quasi-isomorphism on $\operatorname{sk}_nK$.

steps.slogan: Pass from the skeleta to the whole simplicial set $K$.
steps.detail: $A_{PL}(K)=\varprojlim_n A_{PL}(\operatorname{sk}_nK)$ along onto maps, and the same holds for cochains. The relative terms live in degree $n$, so $H^p$ of the skeleta is constant for $n>p+1$. Then the Milnor sequence has no $\varprojlim^1$ term, and $\int$ is a quasi-isomorphism on $K$.

concepts.c:simplicial-set: The proof inducts over the skeleta and simplices of the simplicial set.
concepts.c:simplicial-complex: A simplicial complex gives a simplicial set, so the theorem applies to it.
concepts.c:quasi-isomorphism: The theorem says exactly that integration is a quasi-isomorphism.
concepts.c:polynomial-differential-form: These forms have a Poincaré lemma and restrict onto boundaries of simplices.
concepts.c:cohomology: Both sides of the isomorphism are cohomology groups.
concepts.c:exact-sequence: Long exact sequences let the five lemma compare skeleta.

source.note: The classical proof of Sullivan's PL de Rham theorem: the Poincare lemma, extendability of A_PL and induction over skeleta, as in Felix, Halperin and Thomas, Rational Homotopy Theory (GTM 205), Section 10, and Bousfield and Gugenheim, Memoirs of the AMS 179 (1976).

statement: Let $G$ be a connected [semisimple Lie group](c:semisimple-lie-group) with finite center and maximal compact subgroup $K$. The [spherical function](c:spherical-function) transform of $K$-biinvariant functions extends to a unitary isomorphism from $L^2(K\backslash G/K)$ onto the Weyl-invariant part of $L^2(\mathfrak{a}^*,|c(\lambda)|^{-2}d\lambda)$, where $c$ is Harish-Chandra's $c$-function, up to normalization of measures.

hypotheses.text: $G$ is a connected [semisimple Lie group](c:semisimple-lie-group) with finite center.
$K$ is a maximal compact subgroup of $G$, and $G=KAN$ is an Iwasawa decomposition with $\mathfrak{a}=\operatorname{Lie}A$.
The functions are $K$-biinvariant, that is, $f(k_1gk_2)=f(g)$.

conclusion: The spherical transform $\hat f(\lambda)=\int_G f(g)\,\varphi_{-\lambda}(g)\,dg$ satisfies $\int_G|f|^2dg=C\int_{\mathfrak{a}^*}|\hat f(\lambda)|^2|c(\lambda)|^{-2}d\lambda$, and it is onto the Weyl-invariant functions.

proofs.name: Harish-Chandra's wave packet proof
proofs.slogan: Turn the spherical transform into a Fourier transform of the Abel transform, invert it at the identity, then extend the resulting isometry by density.
proofs.scope: This is an outline of Harish-Chandra's proof for $K$-biinvariant functions, with the steps that rest on the cited work marked in the details. Plancherel formulas for other $K$-types and for the full group are other members of the family.

roles.why: Finite center and semisimplicity give the Iwasawa decomposition, the Abel transform and the $c$-function.
The Iwasawa decomposition $G=KAN$ and the compact $K$ define the spherical functions $\varphi_\lambda$.
Biinvariance makes $f$ a function on $G/K$ whose transform is a function of $\lambda$ alone.

steps.slogan: Write the spherical transform as the Fourier transform of the Abel transform.
steps.detail: For a $K$-biinvariant $f$ put $F_f(a)=e^{\rho(\log a)}\int_Nf(an)\,dn$ on $A\cong\mathfrak{a}$. The integral formula $\varphi_\lambda(g)=\int_Ke^{(i\lambda-\rho)(H(gk))}dk$ gives $\hat f(\lambda)=\int_AF_f(a)\,a^{-i\lambda}\,da$. So $\hat f$ is the Euclidean [Fourier transform](c:fourier-transform) of a Weyl-invariant function.

steps.slogan: Expand the spherical functions on the positive chamber with the $c$-function.
steps.detail: Harish-Chandra proves that $\varphi_\lambda(a)=\sum_{w\in W}c(w\lambda)\,e^{(iw\lambda-\rho)(\log a)}+{}$(a faster decaying term) for $a$ in the positive chamber. The $c$-function is meromorphic, and $|c(\lambda)|^{-2}$ is a tempered density on real $\lambda$. This step rests on the cited work.

steps.slogan: Prove the inversion formula at the identity by a wave packet argument.
steps.detail: For $f\in C_c^\infty(G//K)$, Harish-Chandra studies the wave packets $\int\hat f(\lambda)\varphi_\lambda(g)\,|c(\lambda)|^{-2}d\lambda$ with the expansion of $\varphi_\lambda$ and shows that they reproduce $f$. At $g=e$, where $\varphi_\lambda(e)=1$, this gives $f(e)=C\int_{\mathfrak{a}^*}\hat f(\lambda)\,|c(\lambda)|^{-2}\,d\lambda$. This step rests on the cited work.

steps.slogan: Apply inversion at the identity to $f*f^*$ to get the Plancherel identity.
steps.detail: The function $f*f^*$ is $K$-biinvariant with $\widehat{f*f^*}=|\hat f|^2$ and $(f*f^*)(e)=\int_G|f|^2dg$. Inversion at $e$ gives $\int_G|f|^2dg=C\int|\hat f|^2|c|^{-2}d\lambda$ for every $f\in C_c^\infty(G//K)$.

steps.slogan: Extend the isometry by density and show that its range is everything.
steps.detail: The space $C_c^\infty(G//K)$ is dense in $L^2(G//K)$, so the transform extends to an isometry. Its range contains the Weyl-invariant functions of Paley-Wiener type (Helgason, Gangolli), which are dense in the target. A closed dense range is the whole target, so the isometry is onto.

concepts.c:semisimple-lie-group: The Iwasawa decomposition and the $c$-function exist for these groups.
concepts.c:spherical-function: The spherical functions are the kernels of the transform.
concepts.c:fourier-transform: The spherical transform becomes a Fourier transform on $\mathfrak{a}$ after the Abel transform.

source.ref: Harish-Chandra, Spherical functions on a semisimple Lie group I and II, American Journal of Mathematics 80 (1958), 241-310 and 553-613; see also R. Gangolli and V. S. Varadarajan, Harmonic Analysis of Spherical Functions on Real Reductive Groups, Springer, 1988.
source.note: The steps follow Harish-Chandra's treatment of the spherical transform; the cited work supplies the asymptotic expansion, the inversion formula and the Paley-Wiener range.

statement: Let $a,b,c,d$ lie on one [circle](c:circle), with the diagonals $ac$ and $bd$ of the [cyclic quadrilateral](c:cyclic-quadrilateral) crossing at an interior point $p$. Then $|ab|\,|cd|+|bc|\,|da|=|ac|\,|bd|$, where $|xy|$ is the [distance](c:distance) between $x$ and $y$.

hypotheses.text: The four points $a,b,c,d$ lie on one [circle](c:circle) (in Euclidean space: on one sphere).
The point $p$ lies strictly between $a$ and $c$ and strictly between $b$ and $d$.

conclusion: The product of the diagonals equals the sum of the products of opposite sides.

formal.difference: mathlib works in any real inner product space with four cospherical points and a point $p$ with $\angle apc=\angle bpd=\pi$, because it has no cyclic polygon. This is the same statement for a convex cyclic quadrilateral.

proofs.name: Similar triangles and Stewart's theorem
proofs.slogan: The chords theorem makes two pairs of triangles similar at $p$, and Stewart's theorem on the cevian $bp$ then gives the product formula.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem, in any Euclidean space; degenerate cases with $a=b$ or $c=d$ need no separate argument. Division by $|bp|$ is allowed because $p$ lies strictly between $b$ and $d$.

roles.why: Concyclic points let the intersecting chords theorem give $|ap|\,|pc|=|bp|\,|pd|$.
The point $p$ gives vertical angles at $p$, splits $ac$ and $bd$ into segments, and makes $|bp|\ne0$.

steps.slogan: Equate the products of the diagonal segments at $p$.
steps.detail: The points are on one [circle](c:circle) and $p$ is inside both [chords](c:chord) $ac$ and $bd$. The intersecting chords theorem gives $|ap|\,|pc|=|bp|\,|pd|$.

steps.slogan: Scale triangle $bpa$ by $|cp|/|bp|$ to get triangle $cpd$.
steps.detail: The angles at $p$ are vertical, so $\angle cpd=\angle bpa$. Put $r=|cp|/|bp|$. Then $|cp|=r|bp|$ and, by step 1, $|dp|=r|ap|$. The law of cosines gives $|cd|=r|ab|$, so $|cd|=\frac{|cp|}{|bp|}|ab|$ ([similar triangles](c:similar-triangles)).

steps.slogan: Scale triangle $cpb$ by $|ap|/|bp|$ to get triangle $dpa$.
steps.detail: Again $\angle dpa=\angle cpb$. Put $r=|ap|/|bp|$. Then $|ap|=r|bp|$ and, by step 1, $|dp|=r|cp|$. The law of cosines gives $|da|=r|bc|$, so $|da|=\frac{|ap|}{|bp|}|bc|$.

steps.slogan: Apply Stewart's theorem to the cevian $bp$ of triangle $abc$.
steps.detail: The point $p$ lies on the side $ac$ of triangle $abc$, and Stewart's theorem gives $|ab|^2|pc|+|bc|^2|ap|=|ac|\bigl(|bp|^2+|ap|\,|pc|\bigr)$.

steps.slogan: Substitute the two ratios and the chord relation to reach the product formula.
steps.detail: By steps 2 and 3, $|ab||cd|+|bc||da|=\frac{1}{|bp|}\bigl(|ab|^2|cp|+|bc|^2|ap|\bigr)$. Step 4 and then step 1 turn this into $|ac|\,(|bp|+|dp|)=|ac|\,|bd|$, since $p$ lies between $b$ and $d$.

concepts.c:circle: Points on one circle are what the intersecting chords theorem needs.
concepts.c:cyclic-quadrilateral: The theorem is about the sides and diagonals of this quadrilateral.
concepts.c:distance: All quantities in the formula are distances between the four points.
concepts.c:chord: The diagonals are chords that meet at $p$.
concepts.c:similar-triangles: Similar triangles at $p$ convert the sides into ratios of segments.

statement: Let $\mathcal{A}$ be a small [abelian category](c:abelian-category) and $\mathcal{B}$ a nonempty full subcategory closed under subobjects, quotients and finite products. If every object of $\mathcal{A}$ has a finite [filtration](c:filtration) with successive quotients in $\mathcal{B}$, then the inclusion induces isomorphisms $K_n(\mathcal{B})\to K_n(\mathcal{A})$ for all $n\ge0$.

hypotheses.text: $\mathcal{A}$ is a small [abelian category](c:abelian-category).
$\mathcal{B}$ is a nonempty full subcategory of $\mathcal{A}$, closed under subobjects, quotients and finite products.
Every object of $\mathcal{A}$ has a finite [filtration](c:filtration) whose successive quotients lie in $\mathcal{B}$.

conclusion: The inclusion $\mathcal{B}\hookrightarrow\mathcal{A}$ induces isomorphisms of [algebraic K-theory](c:algebraic-k-theory) groups $K_n(\mathcal{B})\cong K_n(\mathcal{A})$ for every $n\ge0$.

proofs.name: Quillen's Theorem A on the Q-construction
proofs.slogan: Show that the inclusion of Q-categories has contractible comma categories, so Theorem A makes it a homotopy equivalence.
proofs.scope: This is an outline of Quillen's proof. The step that proves contractibility by induction on the filtration length rests on the cited paper.

roles.why: Both $\mathcal{A}$ and $\mathcal{B}$ are exact categories, so the $Q$-construction and the K-groups are defined.
Closure under subobjects and quotients makes $\mathcal{B}$ exact and describes the comma categories as subquotients in $\mathcal{B}$.
The finite filtrations give the induction on length that proves contractibility.

steps.slogan: Pass to the Q-construction, whose loop space gives K-theory.
steps.detail: Quillen defines $K_n(\mathcal{C})=\pi_{n+1}(BQ\mathcal{C},0)$ for an exact category $\mathcal{C}$. A morphism $M\to N$ in $Q\mathcal{C}$ is a diagram $M\twoheadleftarrow N'\hookrightarrow N$. The inclusion $i$ is exact, so it induces $Qi\colon Q\mathcal{B}\to Q\mathcal{A}$.

steps.slogan: Reduce to contractibility of the comma categories of $Qi$.
steps.detail: Quillen's Theorem A says that a functor whose comma categories $f/d$ are all contractible is a homotopy equivalence on classifying spaces. So it suffices to show that $Qi/M$ is contractible for each object $M$ of $\mathcal{A}$.

steps.slogan: Describe the objects of the comma category as subquotients of $M$ that lie in $\mathcal{B}$.
steps.detail: An object of $Qi/M$ is an object $N$ of $\mathcal{B}$ with a morphism $N\to M$ in $Q\mathcal{A}$, that is, a subobject $M'\subseteq M$ with a quotient $M'\twoheadrightarrow N$. Closure of $\mathcal{B}$ under subobjects and quotients keeps all the data inside $\mathcal{B}$.

steps.slogan: Prove contractibility by induction on the length of a filtration of $M$.
steps.detail: If $M$ lies in $\mathcal{B}$, the identity of $M$ is a terminal object and $Qi/M$ is contractible. In general Quillen uses a filtration of $M$ with quotients in $\mathcal{B}$ to compare $Qi/M$ with the comma categories of the shorter pieces. This step rests on the cited paper.

steps.slogan: Conclude that $BQ\mathcal{B}\to BQ\mathcal{A}$ is a homotopy equivalence.
steps.detail: Theorem A applies to $Qi$ by step 4, so $BQi$ is a homotopy equivalence. Hence $K_n(\mathcal{B})=\pi_{n+1}BQ\mathcal{B}\to\pi_{n+1}BQ\mathcal{A}=K_n(\mathcal{A})$ is an isomorphism for every $n\ge0$.

concepts.c:abelian-category: An abelian category is an exact category, so it has K-groups.
concepts.c:filtration: Finite filtrations by objects of the subcategory drive the induction.
concepts.c:algebraic-k-theory: The theorem compares these groups for the two categories.

source.ref: D. Quillen, Higher algebraic K-theory I, in Algebraic K-theory I (Seattle 1972), Lecture Notes in Mathematics 341, Springer, 1973, pp. 85-147, Section 5, Theorem 4.
source.note: Quillen's proof of dévissage by Theorem A. Weibel, The K-book, Chapter V, gives another account.

statement: Let $X$ be a nonsingular variety over a field, $V,W\subseteq X$ closed subvarieties and $Z$ an irreducible component of $V\cap W$ with $\operatorname{codim}Z=\operatorname{codim}V+\operatorname{codim}W$. Then the multiplicity of $Z$ in the product $V\cdot W$ in the [Chow group](c:chow-group) is $\sum_{i\ge0}(-1)^i\,\ell\bigl(\operatorname{Tor}_i^{\mathcal{O}_{X,Z}}(\mathcal{O}_{V,Z},\mathcal{O}_{W,Z})\bigr)$.

hypotheses.text: $X$ is a nonsingular variety over a field, so $\mathcal{O}_{X,Z}$ is a [regular local ring](c:is-regular-local-ring).
The intersection is proper along $Z$: $\operatorname{codim}Z=\operatorname{codim}V+\operatorname{codim}W$.

conclusion: The [intersection multiplicity](c:intersection-multiplicity) of $Z$ in $V\cdot W$ equals the alternating sum of the lengths of the [Tor](c:tor-functor) modules.

proofs.name: Diagonal, normal cone and Koszul complex
proofs.slogan: Reduce to the diagonal, read the multiplicity as the Samuel multiplicity of the normal cone, and equate it with the Koszul Euler characteristic that computes Tor.
proofs.scope: This is an outline of Fulton's proof of the Tor formula; the equality of the multiplicity with the Samuel multiplicity and Serre's multiplicity theorem rest on the cited works. Serre's vanishing and positivity statements for regular local rings are other members of the family.

roles.why: Nonsingularity makes the diagonal a regular embedding cut out locally by a regular sequence.
Proper intersection makes the normal cone of pure dimension and the multiplicity a finite number.

steps.slogan: Write the intersection product as a refined Gysin pullback along the diagonal.
steps.detail: Let $\Delta\colon X\to X\times X$ be the diagonal. Since $X$ is nonsingular, $\Delta$ is a regular embedding, and the product is defined by $V\cdot W=\Delta^![V\times W]$ in the [Chow group](c:chow-group), through the normal cone of $V\cap W$ in $V\times W$.

steps.slogan: Read the multiplicity of $Z$ as the Samuel multiplicity of the diagonal ideal.
steps.detail: Proper intersection gives the part of the normal cone over $Z$ the dimension of the normal bundle there, so it is $m$ times the bundle, and $m$ is the multiplicity of $Z$. Here $m$ is the Samuel multiplicity $e(I,B)$ of the diagonal ideal $I$ in the local ring $B$ of $V\times W$ at the generic point of $Z$. This step rests on the cited work.

steps.slogan: Identify the Tor modules with the homology of a Koszul complex.
steps.detail: Locally the ideal $I$ is generated by a regular sequence $f_1,\dots,f_d$ with $d=\dim X$. Serre's reduction to the diagonal gives $\operatorname{Tor}_i^{\mathcal{O}_{X,Z}}(\mathcal{O}_{V,Z},\mathcal{O}_{W,Z})\cong H_i(f_1,\dots,f_d;B)$, the homology of the [Koszul complex](c:koszul-complex).

steps.slogan: Equate the Samuel multiplicity with the Euler characteristic of the Koszul complex.
steps.detail: The elements $f_1,\dots,f_d$ form a system of parameters of $B$ with $d=\dim B$ by proper intersection. Serre's theorem in local algebra gives $\sum_i(-1)^i\,\ell\,H_i(f_1,\dots,f_d;B)=e(I,B)$. This step rests on the cited work.

steps.slogan: Chain the three equalities to get the Tor formula.
steps.detail: Step 2 gives multiplicity $=e(I,B)$, step 4 gives $e(I,B)=\sum(-1)^i\ell\,H_i(f;B)$, and step 3 identifies this sum with $\sum(-1)^i\ell\bigl(\operatorname{Tor}_i\bigr)$.

concepts.c:chow-group: The product $V\cdot W$ and the multiplicity of $Z$ live in the Chow group.
concepts.c:is-regular-local-ring: Regularity makes the diagonal ideal a regular sequence and Tor finite.
concepts.c:intersection-multiplicity: The multiplicity of $Z$ in $V\cdot W$ is the quantity computed.
concepts.c:tor-functor: The lengths of the Tor modules form the alternating sum.
concepts.c:koszul-complex: Its homology is the Tor of the two coordinate rings.

source.ref: W. Fulton, Intersection Theory, second edition, Springer, 1998, Chapter 7 (Proposition 7.1); J.-P. Serre, Algèbre locale, multiplicités, Lecture Notes in Mathematics 11, Springer, 1965, Chapters IV and V.
source.note: Fulton derives the Tor formula from the normal cone definition of the product; Serre proves the reduction to the diagonal and the multiplicity theorem for Koszul complexes.

statement: Let $K$ be a field of characteristic zero and $(a_n)_{n\ge0}$ a sequence in $K$ with $a_{n+k}=c_{k-1}a_{n+k-1}+\dots+c_0a_n$ for constants $c_i\in K$. Then $\{n:a_n=0\}$ is the union of a finite set and finitely many [arithmetic progressions](c:arithmetic-progression).

hypotheses.text: The field $K$ has characteristic zero.
The sequence satisfies a [linear recurrence](c:linear-recurrence) of order $k$ with constant coefficients in $K$.

conclusion: The set of indices $n$ with $a_n=0$ is a finite set together with finitely many progressions $\{r+mN:m\ge0\}$.

proofs.name: Lech's p-adic proof
proofs.slogan: Embed the data in the $p$-adic integers, write each residue class of the sequence as a $p$-adic power series, and count its zeros with Strassmann's theorem.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem; a recurrence with $c_0=0$ is first shortened, which changes finitely many terms. The embedding of a finitely generated ring into $\mathbb{Z}_p$ is quoted from Cassels.

roles.why: The recurrence turns the sequence into $a_n=e_1^{T}M^nv_0$ for the companion [matrix](c:matrix) $M$.
Only a ring of characteristic zero embeds in $\mathbb{Z}_p$, and the embedding keeps zeros as zeros.

steps.slogan: Write the sequence through powers of the companion matrix $M$.
steps.detail: Put $v_n=(a_n,\dots,a_{n+k-1})^T$, so $v_n=M^nv_0$ and $a_n=e_1^TM^nv_0$. If $c_0=0$, the shifted sequence satisfies a recurrence of order $k-1$; repeat. This changes finitely many indices, or the sequence vanishes from some index on. So assume $c_0\ne0$ and $M$ invertible.

steps.slogan: Embed the finitely generated ring of the data into the $p$-adic integers.
steps.detail: The ring $R=\mathbb{Z}[c_0^{-1},c_0,\dots,c_{k-1},a_0,\dots,a_{k-1}]\subseteq K$ is a finitely generated domain of characteristic zero. Cassels' embedding lemma gives an odd prime $p$ and an injective ring map $R\hookrightarrow\mathbb{Z}_p$. Then $M\in GL_k(\mathbb{Z}_p)$ and the zeros of $a_n$ are unchanged. Assume $K=\mathbb{Q}_p$.

steps.slogan: Split the indices into residue classes along which $M^n$ is close to the identity.
steps.detail: The group $GL_k(\mathbb{Z}/p)$ is finite, so $M^N\equiv I\pmod p$ for some $N\ge1$. Write $M^N=I+pB$ with $B$ integral. For $0\le r<N$ we get $a_{r+mN}=e_1^TM^r(I+pB)^mv_0$.

steps.slogan: Show that $m\mapsto a_{r+mN}$ is one convergent power series on $\mathbb{Z}_p$.
steps.detail: For odd $p$, $\log(I+pB)=\sum_{j\ge1}(-1)^{j-1}(pB)^j/j$ converges and $(I+pB)^m=\exp\bigl(m\log(I+pB)\bigr)=\sum_jC_jm^j$ with $C_j=\log(I+pB)^j/j!\to0$. So $a_{r+mN}=\sum_j\gamma_jm^j$ with $\gamma_j\in\mathbb{Z}_p$ and $\gamma_j\to0$, a [power series](c:power-series) converging on all of $\mathbb{Z}_p$.

steps.slogan: Count the zeros of each series with Strassmann's theorem.
steps.detail: A nonzero power series over $\mathbb{Z}_p$ with coefficients tending to zero has only finitely many zeros in $\mathbb{Z}_p$. So in each class $r$, either $a_{r+mN}=0$ for finitely many $m$, or the series is zero and $a_{r+mN}=0$ for every $m$.

steps.slogan: Collect the residue classes into a finite set and progressions.
steps.detail: Classes with finitely many zeros add a finite set. Classes with the zero series add the full progressions $\{r+mN:m\ge0\}$. Adding the finitely many indices dropped in step 1 gives the claimed form.

concepts.c:linear-recurrence: The recurrence gives the matrix power form of the sequence.
concepts.c:arithmetic-progression: The infinite zero classes are arithmetic progressions.
concepts.c:matrix: The companion matrix carries the recurrence, and its powers give the terms.
concepts.c:power-series: Each residue class becomes a convergent power series in $m$.

source.note: The p-adic proof of C. Lech, A note on recurring series, Arkiv for Matematik 2 (1953), 417-421, with the embedding lemma of J. W. S. Cassels, An embedding theorem for fields, Bull. Austral. Math. Soc. 14 (1976), 193-198.

statement: Let a [Lie group](c:lie-group) $G$ act smoothly and properly on a manifold $M$, let $x\in M$ and $H=G_x$. Then $H$ is compact, the [orbit](c:orbit) $G\cdot x$ is a closed embedded submanifold, and for an $H$-invariant ball $B$ in $N_x=T_xM/T_x(G\cdot x)$ there is a $G$-equivariant diffeomorphism from $G\times_HB$ onto a $G$-invariant open neighbourhood of $G\cdot x$.

hypotheses.text: A [Lie group](c:lie-group) $G$ acts smoothly on a smooth manifold $M$.
The action is [proper](c:proper-action): $(g,y)\mapsto(gy,y)$ is a proper map.

conclusion: The orbit is closed and embedded, $H$ is compact, and a neighbourhood of the orbit is $G$-equivariantly $G\times_HB$.

proofs.name: Invariant metric and normal exponential map
proofs.slogan: Make the metric invariant, identify the normal bundle of the orbit with $G\times_HN_x$, and show that the normal exponential map is an embedding on a disc bundle.
proofs.scope: The whole statement, for any dimension; if $G$ is compact, properness is automatic. A small enough radius $\varepsilon$ works for the entire orbit because $G$ acts transitively on it.

roles.why: Smoothness gives the orbit map, its immersion property and the equivariance of the exponential map.
Properness gives a compact stabilizer, an embedded orbit, an invariant metric and the injectivity of exp.

steps.slogan: Show that the stabilizer is compact and the orbit is a closed embedded submanifold.
steps.detail: The map $(g,y)\mapsto(gy,y)$ is proper, so $H\times\{x\}$, the preimage of $(x,x)$, is compact. The orbit map induces an injective immersion $G/H\to M$. Properness shows that its image is closed and that the map is an embedding.

steps.slogan: Average a Riemannian metric to make the action isometric.
steps.detail: A proper action has a cutoff function $c\ge0$ with $\int_Gc(g^{-1}y)\,dg=1$ for all $y$. For a [Riemannian](c:riemannian-manifold) metric $\langle\,,\rangle$ on $M$, the weighted average $\int_Gc(g^{-1}y)\,\langle g^{-1}_*\cdot,g^{-1}_*\cdot\rangle_{g^{-1}y}\,dg$ is a $G$-invariant metric.

steps.slogan: Identify the normal bundle of the orbit with $G\times_HN_x$.
steps.detail: The group $H$ acts on $T_xM$ by isometries that preserve $T_x(G\cdot x)$, so it acts on the orthogonal complement $N_x\cong T_xM/T_x(G\cdot x)$. The map $[g,v]\mapsto g_*v$ is a $G$-equivariant isomorphism from $G\times_HN_x$ onto the [normal bundle](c:normal-bundle) $\nu$ of the orbit.

steps.slogan: Choose a radius on which the normal exponential map is a local diffeomorphism.
steps.detail: Since $G$ acts by isometries, $\exp\colon\nu\to M$ is $G$-equivariant, and its differential is invertible along the zero section. The set where $d\exp$ is invertible is open and $G$-invariant, and $G$ is transitive on the orbit, so it contains the disc bundle $\nu_\varepsilon$ for one $\varepsilon>0$.

steps.slogan: Prove that $\exp$ is injective on a smaller disc bundle by a properness argument.
steps.detail: Otherwise there are $v_n\ne w_n$ with $|v_n|,|w_n|\to0$ and $\exp v_n=\exp w_n$. Move $v_n$ over $x$ by the group; then the base points $h_nx$ of $w_n$ tend to $x$. Properness gives $h_n\to h\in H$ along a subsequence, so $v_n,w_n\to0_x$, where $\exp$ is injective. This is a contradiction.

steps.slogan: Restrict to a ball and read off the equivariant diffeomorphism.
steps.detail: Take an $H$-invariant ball $B\subset N_x$ of radius $\varepsilon'$. By step 3, $G\times_HB$ is the disc bundle $\nu_{\varepsilon'}$, on which $\exp$ is an injective local diffeomorphism. So $\exp$ is a $G$-equivariant diffeomorphism onto a $G$-invariant open neighbourhood of $G\cdot x$ (a [tubular neighbourhood](c:tubular-neighbourhood)).

concepts.c:lie-group: The group acts smoothly and has a Haar measure for averaging.
concepts.c:orbit: The theorem describes a neighbourhood of one orbit.
concepts.c:lie-group-action: Smoothness of the action gives the orbit map and equivariant exponential map.
concepts.c:proper-action: Properness gives compact stabilizers, closed orbits and the injectivity radius.
concepts.c:riemannian-manifold: An invariant Riemannian metric makes the group act by isometries.
concepts.c:normal-bundle: The normal bundle of the orbit is the object that exp embeds.
concepts.c:tubular-neighbourhood: The disc bundle image is an equivariant tubular neighbourhood of the orbit.

source.note: The proof is Palais's: an invariant metric and the normal exponential map, as in R. S. Palais, On the existence of slices for actions of non-compact Lie groups, Annals of Mathematics 73 (1961), 295-323.

statement: Let $A$ be a [finite](c:finite-set) subset of a [group](c:group) with $A^{-1}=A$ and $|A^3|\le K|A|$. Then $|A^m|\le K^{m-2}|A|$ for every integer $m\ge3$.

hypotheses.text: $A$ is a finite [symmetric](c:symmetric-set) subset of a group $G$, that is, $A^{-1}=A$.
The tripling constant satisfies $|A^3|\le K|A|$ for a real number $K$.
The exponent $m$ is an integer with $m\ge3$.

proofs.name: Ruzsa triangle inequality and induction
proofs.slogan: Prove the bound for all products of $m$ factors $A^{\pm1}$ by induction on $m$, splitting a long product and applying Ruzsa's triangle inequality.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem, including $A=\emptyset$, where both sides are $0$. The generalization to products with signs $\pm1$ is what makes the induction work.

roles.why: Symmetry makes every product of $m$ factors $A^{\pm1}$ equal to $A^m$, so signs cost nothing.
The tripling bound is the base case $m=3$ of the induction.
The induction starts at $m=3$ and each step increases $m$ by one.

steps.slogan: Generalize to products of $m$ factors $A^{\pm1}$ and induct on $m$.
steps.detail: For $\varepsilon\in\{\pm1\}^m$ write $A^\varepsilon=A^{\varepsilon_1}\cdots A^{\varepsilon_m}$. We prove $|A^\varepsilon|\le K^{m-2}|A|$ for all $\varepsilon$ by induction on $m\ge3$. Because $A$ is [symmetric](c:symmetric-set), every $A^\varepsilon$ equals $A^m$, so this contains the theorem.

steps.slogan: Settle $m=3$ from the tripling hypothesis.
steps.detail: For every sign pattern, $A^{\varepsilon_1}A^{\varepsilon_2}A^{\varepsilon_3}=A^3$, because each $A^{\pm1}$ equals $A$ by symmetry. So $|A^\varepsilon|=|A^3|\le K|A|=K^{3-2}|A|$, which is the claim for $m=3$.

steps.slogan: Split a product of $m+1$ factors as $V^{-1}W$.
steps.detail: Take $\varepsilon\in\{\pm1\}^{m+1}$ and put $V=A^{-\varepsilon_2}A^{-\varepsilon_1}$ and $W=A^{\varepsilon_3}\cdots A^{\varepsilon_{m+1}}$. Then $V^{-1}=A^{\varepsilon_1}A^{\varepsilon_2}$, so $V^{-1}W=A^\varepsilon$.

steps.slogan: Bound the full product by Ruzsa's triangle inequality.
steps.detail: Ruzsa's triangle inequality gives $|A|\,|V^{-1}W|\le|AV|\,|AW|$. Here $AV=A\,A^{-\varepsilon_2}A^{-\varepsilon_1}$ has three factors and $AW=A\,A^{\varepsilon_3}\cdots A^{\varepsilon_{m+1}}$ has $m$ factors.

steps.slogan: Bound both factors and divide by $|A|$.
steps.detail: The three-factor product has size at most $K|A|$ by step 2. The $m$-factor product has size at most $K^{m-2}|A|$ by the induction hypothesis. So $|A|\,|A^\varepsilon|\le K^{m-1}|A|^2$, and for $A\ne\emptyset$ division by $|A|$ gives $|A^\varepsilon|\le K^{(m+1)-2}|A|$.

concepts.c:symmetric-set: Symmetry turns every signed product into the plain power $A^m$.
concepts.c:group: Inverses of products and Ruzsa's inequality need a group.
concepts.c:finite-set: Cardinalities are finite, so the inequalities are between numbers.

statement: Let $G$ be a connected complex reductive group with [Weyl group](c:weyl-group) $W$. The pushforward of the constant sheaf along the Springer resolution $T^*(G/B)\to\mathcal{N}$ of the nilpotent cone is a [perverse sheaf](c:perverse-sheaf) $\bigoplus_{\chi\in\operatorname{Irr}W}V_\chi\otimes IC(\mathcal{O}_\chi,\mathcal{L}_\chi)$, and $\chi\mapsto(\mathcal{O}_\chi,\mathcal{L}_\chi)$ is injective.

hypotheses.text: $G$ is a connected reductive algebraic group over $\mathbb{C}$, with [flag variety](c:flag-variety) $G/B$ and Weyl group $W$.

conclusion: Each irreducible $W$-module $V_\chi$ corresponds to a pair of a [nilpotent orbit](c:nilpotent-orbit) $\mathcal{O}_\chi$ and an irreducible equivariant [local system](c:local-system), and distinct modules give distinct pairs.

proofs.name: Semismall resolution and the decomposition theorem
proofs.slogan: The Springer resolution is semismall, so its pushforward splits into simple perverse sheaves, and the Steinberg variety shows that the multiplicity algebra is the group algebra of $W$.
proofs.scope: This is an outline of the Borho-MacPherson and Lusztig proof, with coefficients in $\mathbb{C}$. Lusztig's generalized Springer correspondence, which adds the pairs not in the image, and the version in positive characteristic are other members of the family.

roles.why: Reductivity gives the Weyl group, the flag variety, the nilpotent cone and the Steinberg variety.

steps.slogan: Set up the Springer resolution of the nilpotent cone.
steps.detail: The variety $\tilde{\mathcal{N}}=T^*(G/B)=G\times_B\mathfrak{n}$ is smooth of dimension $\dim\mathcal{N}$. The map $\pi(g,x)=\operatorname{Ad}(g)x$ is proper and birational onto $\mathcal{N}$, and its fibres are the Springer fibres $\mathcal{B}_u$.

steps.slogan: Show that the Springer resolution is semismall with every orbit relevant.
steps.detail: Steinberg's dimension formula gives $\dim\mathcal{B}_u=\tfrac12\operatorname{codim}_{\mathcal{N}}\mathcal{O}_u$ for every $u\in\mathcal{N}$. So $\pi$ is semismall, and every nilpotent orbit is relevant. This step rests on the cited work.

steps.slogan: Split the pushforward into simple perverse sheaves by the decomposition theorem.
steps.detail: For a semismall proper map from a smooth variety, $\pi_*\mathbb{C}[\dim\tilde{\mathcal{N}}]$ is perverse. By the decomposition theorem it is a direct sum of terms $V_{\mathcal{O},\mathcal{L}}\otimes IC(\mathcal{O},\mathcal{L})$ over pairs of an orbit and an irreducible equivariant local system.

steps.slogan: Compute the endomorphism algebra with the Steinberg variety.
steps.detail: The algebra $\operatorname{End}(\pi_*\mathbb{C})$ is the top Borel-Moore homology $H_{top}(Z)$ of the Steinberg variety $Z=\tilde{\mathcal{N}}\times_{\mathcal{N}}\tilde{\mathcal{N}}$ with convolution. Its irreducible components are indexed by $W$ and $H_{top}(Z)\cong\mathbb{C}[W]$ as algebras. This step rests on the cited work.

steps.slogan: Match the simple summands with the irreducible $W$-modules.
steps.detail: By step 3 the endomorphism algebra is $\prod\operatorname{End}(V_{\mathcal{O},\mathcal{L}})$, and by step 4 it is $\mathbb{C}[W]$. So the $V_{\mathcal{O},\mathcal{L}}$ that occur are exactly the irreducible $W$-modules $V_\chi$, each once, and different $\chi$ give different pairs.

concepts.c:weyl-group: Its irreducible modules are the objects matched with sheaves.
concepts.c:perverse-sheaf: Semismallness makes the pushforward a perverse sheaf that splits.
concepts.c:flag-variety: The Springer resolution is built from the cotangent bundle of $G/B$.
concepts.c:nilpotent-orbit: The supports of the summands are closures of nilpotent orbits.
concepts.c:local-system: Each summand is the intersection complex of a local system on an orbit.

source.ref: N. Chriss and V. Ginzburg, Representation Theory and Complex Geometry, Birkhäuser, 1997, Chapter 3; W. Borho and R. MacPherson, Partial resolutions of nilpotent varieties, Astérisque 101-102 (1983), 23-74.
source.note: Chriss and Ginzburg derive the correspondence from the Steinberg variety and the decomposition theorem; Borho and MacPherson use the semismall resolution.

statement: Let $f$ be a [modular form](c:modular-form) of level one and weight $k\in\mathbb{N}$. If its [q-expansion](c:q-expansion) has order greater than $\lfloor k/12\rfloor$, then $f=0$.

hypotheses.text: $f$ is a [modular form](c:modular-form) for $\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb{Z})$ of natural weight $k$.
The [q-expansion](c:q-expansion) of $f$ at $\infty$ has order greater than $\lfloor k/12\rfloor$.

proofs.name: Division by the discriminant form
proofs.slogan: Divide the cusp form by $\Delta$ to lower the weight by $12$ and the order by $1$, and use induction on the weight.
proofs.scope: All natural weights, including $k=0$ and odd $k$, by strong induction on $k$. Weights below $12$ end at forms of negative weight, which vanish.

roles.why: Level-one weight-$k$ forms are the objects that division by $\Delta$ moves to weight $k-12$.
The order bound makes $f$ a [cusp form](c:cusp-form) and passes to the quotient with order lowered by one.

steps.slogan: Argue by strong induction on the weight $k$.
steps.detail: Assume the statement for all natural weights below $k$. Let $f$ have weight $k$ and $q$-order greater than $\lfloor k/12\rfloor$.

steps.slogan: Show that $f$ is a cusp form.
steps.detail: The order is greater than $\lfloor k/12\rfloor\ge0$, so it is at least $1$. Hence the constant coefficient of the q-expansion is $0$, and $f$ is a [cusp form](c:cusp-form).

steps.slogan: Divide the cusp form by the discriminant form $\Delta$.
steps.detail: The form $\Delta$ has weight $12$, no zeros in the upper half plane and a simple zero at $\infty$. So $g=f/\Delta$ is holomorphic of weight $k-12$ and bounded at $\infty$, because $f$ vanishes there. Thus $g$ is a modular form of weight $k-12$ with $f=\Delta g$.

steps.slogan: For weight below $12$, show that $g$ has negative weight and vanishes.
steps.detail: Level-one forms of weight at most $0$ are constant: the q-expansion function on the unit disc attains its maximum modulus on $|q|\le e^{-\pi}$, so the maximum modulus principle applies. A nonzero constant has weight $0$, so $g=0$ when $k-12<0$.

steps.slogan: For weight at least $12$, lower the order by one and apply induction.
steps.detail: The q-expansions satisfy $q(f)=q(\Delta)\,q(g)$ and $\operatorname{ord}q(\Delta)=1$. So $\operatorname{ord}q(g)=\operatorname{ord}q(f)-1>\lfloor(k-12)/12\rfloor$. The weight $k-12$ is a smaller natural number, so induction gives $g=0$.

steps.slogan: Combine the two weight cases to get $f=0$.
steps.detail: If $k<12$, then $g=0$ by step 4. If $k\ge12$, then $g=0$ by step 5. In both cases $f=\Delta g=0$.

concepts.c:modular-form: Division by $\Delta$ keeps the space of level-one modular forms.
concepts.c:q-expansion: The order of the q-expansion at infinity is the quantity that drops by one.
concepts.c:cusp-form: Vanishing at infinity is what allows division by $\Delta$.

source.note: mathlib inducts on k with CuspForm.discriminantEquiv, levelOne_neg_weight_rank_zero, qExpansion_eq_qExpansion_discriminant_mul and discriminant_qExpansion_order.

proofs.name: Valence formula
proofs.slogan: A nonzero level-one form has total zero weight $k/12$, so its order at infinity cannot exceed $k/12$.
proofs.scope: All natural weights at once; no induction and no case split. The valence formula holds for every nonzero level-one form.

roles.why: A holomorphic form of weight $k$ has nonnegative orders, and the valence formula totals them to $k/12$.
The assumed order exceeds $k/12$ and conflicts with the valence formula.

steps.slogan: Assume that $f$ is nonzero and look for a contradiction.
steps.detail: Suppose $f\ne0$ with $\operatorname{ord}_qf>\lfloor k/12\rfloor$. The order is an integer, so $\operatorname{ord}_qf\ge\lfloor k/12\rfloor+1>k/12$.

steps.slogan: Apply the valence formula to the nonzero form.
steps.detail: For a nonzero level-one form of weight $k$, $v_\infty(f)+\tfrac12v_i(f)+\tfrac13v_\rho(f)+\sum_pv_p(f)=k/12$. The sum runs over the other points $p$ of $\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb{Z})\backslash\mathbb{H}$, and $v_\infty(f)=\operatorname{ord}_qf$.

steps.slogan: Bound the other terms below by zero.
steps.detail: A holomorphic form has no poles, so the orders $v_i(f),v_\rho(f),v_p(f)$ are all at least $0$. Dropping these terms from the valence formula gives $v_\infty(f)\le k/12$.

steps.slogan: Compare the two bounds on $\operatorname{ord}_qf$.
steps.detail: Step 1 gives $v_\infty(f)>k/12$ and step 3 gives $v_\infty(f)\le k/12$. This contradiction shows that $f=0$.

concepts.c:modular-form: The valence formula counts zeros of a nonzero level-one modular form.
concepts.c:q-expansion: The order of the q-expansion at infinity is the zero order at the cusp.

source.note: The classical proof by the valence formula, as in J.-P. Serre, A Course in Arithmetic, Chapter VII, Section 3, Theorem 3.

statement: In a [cut-free](c:cut-free-proof) derivation $D$ in the [sequent calculus](c:sequent-calculus) LK, every [formula](c:formula) occurring in $D$ is a subformula of a formula of the end-sequent, where the instances of a quantified formula count as its subformulas.

hypotheses.text: $D$ is a derivation of a sequent $S$ in the [sequent calculus](c:sequent-calculus) LK, built from axioms by the rules of LK.
$D$ is [cut-free](c:cut-free-proof): it contains no application of the cut rule.

conclusion: Every formula in every sequent of $D$ is a subformula of a formula in $S$.

proofs.name: Induction down the derivation tree
proofs.slogan: Every rule except cut has premise formulas among the subformulas of its conclusion, so the property passes from the end-sequent up to every sequent.
proofs.scope: Propositional and first-order LK with the usual rules; extra axioms or rules need their own local check. The relation is a subformula up to substitution of terms for the bound variable.

roles.why: The derivation is a finite tree, so induction on the depth of a sequent covers all of it.
Cut is the only rule whose premise formula can be absent from its conclusion.

steps.slogan: Define the subformula relation with instances and note that it is transitive.
steps.detail: Say $A\preceq B$ when $A=B$, or $A$ is an immediate part of a formula $C$ with $C\preceq B$. The immediate parts of $B_1\wedge B_2$ are $B_1,B_2$ (likewise for the other [connectives](c:logical-connective)), and those of $\forall xB(x)$ and $\exists xB(x)$ are all instances $B(t)$. The relation is reflexive and transitive.

steps.slogan: Check that every rule except cut has premise formulas that are subformulas of its conclusion formulas.
steps.detail: Axioms have no premises. Weakening, contraction and exchange only copy or move formulas. A rule for a connective or quantifier has as premise formulas the side formulas, which stay in the conclusion, and the immediate parts of the principal formula, which are subformulas of it. Cut fails this test, because its cut formula leaves the conclusion.

steps.slogan: Induct on the depth of a sequent to pass the property from the root to every leaf.
steps.detail: The end-sequent satisfies the claim by reflexivity. A sequent at depth $n+1$ is a premise of a rule at depth $n$, and that rule is not a cut. By step 2 its formulas are subformulas of conclusion formulas, hence of formulas in $S$ by transitivity.

concepts.c:cut-free-proof: Absence of cut is the condition that makes the local check succeed.
concepts.c:sequent-calculus: The rules of the calculus are checked one by one.
concepts.c:formula: The claim is about the formulas inside the derivation.
concepts.c:logical-connective: Each connective rule gives premises that are immediate parts of the principal formula.

source.note: The standard observation after Gentzen's cut elimination theorem (Untersuchungen ueber das logische Schliessen, Math. Z. 39 (1935), 176-210 and 405-431); see Troelstra and Schwichtenberg, Basic Proof Theory, 2nd edition, Cambridge University Press, 2000.

statement: Let $L_1,\dots,L_n$ be linearly independent linear forms in $n\ge2$ variables with real [algebraic](c:algebraic-number) coefficients, and $\varepsilon>0$. The points $x\in\mathbb{Z}^n\setminus\{0\}$ with $|L_1(x)\cdots L_n(x)|<\|x\|^{-\varepsilon}$ lie in finitely many proper [linear subspaces](c:linear-subspace) of $\mathbb{Q}^n$, where $\|x\|=\max|x_i|$.

hypotheses.text: $L_1,\dots,L_n$ are linearly independent linear forms in $n\ge2$ variables with real [algebraic](c:algebraic-number) coefficients.
The exponent $\varepsilon$ is a positive real number.

conclusion: All integer solutions of the inequality lie in the union of finitely many proper [linear subspaces](c:linear-subspace) of $\mathbb{Q}^n$.

proofs.name: Schmidt's method with auxiliary polynomials
proofs.slogan: Place each solution in a thin parallelepiped, confine the lattice points of each parallelepiped to a proper subspace, and show by Roth's method that only finitely many such subspaces occur.
proofs.scope: This is an outline of Schmidt's proof of the real case over $\mathbb{Q}$, and the steps that rest on the cited work are marked. The number field versions with the projective height and Schlickewei's version with several places are the other members of the family.

roles.why: Independence and algebraicity of the forms give a lattice-point count in each parallelepiped and make the auxiliary polynomial argument work.
The positive $\varepsilon$ makes the parallelepipeds have volume bounded by a negative power of the height.

steps.slogan: Turn each solution into a lattice point of a thin parallelepiped.
steps.detail: For a solution $x$ choose exponents $c_1,\dots,c_n$ on a fixed finite grid with $\sum c_i\approx-\varepsilon$ and $|L_i(x)|\le\|x\|^{c_i}$. With $Q=\|x\|$, the point $x$ lies in the [convex body](c:convex-body) $\Pi(Q)=\{y:|L_i(y)|\le Q^{c_i}\}$ of volume about $Q^{-\varepsilon}$. Treat each grid vector separately.

steps.slogan: Confine the lattice points of each body to a proper subspace by Minkowski's second theorem.
steps.detail: The volume of $\Pi(Q)$ is small, so the product of the successive minima is large while the first minimum is at most $1$. Hence the integer points of $\Pi(Q)$ lie in a proper subspace $T(Q)$ spanned by the points of the small minima.

steps.slogan: Reduce the theorem to showing that only finitely many subspaces $T(Q)$ occur.
steps.detail: If infinitely many different $T(Q)$ occur, choose heights $Q_1\ll Q_2\ll\cdots$ and solutions $x^{(j)}$ in distinct subspaces. Schmidt derives a contradiction from the tuple $(x^{(1)},\dots,x^{(m)})$ for $m$ large. This step rests on the cited work.

steps.slogan: Construct an auxiliary multihomogeneous polynomial with Siegel's lemma.
steps.detail: Siegel's lemma gives a nonzero integer polynomial in $m$ groups of $n$ variables, of degrees $r_j\sim1/\log Q_j$, that vanishes to a high weighted index at the tuple of the points $x^{(j)}$, measured in the coordinates $L_i$. Its coefficients are small. This step rests on the cited work.

steps.slogan: Bound the index of the polynomial by Roth's lemma and contradict its construction.
steps.detail: Schmidt's generalization of Roth's lemma bounds the index of such a polynomial at a tuple of independent points. The smallness of the $L_i(x^{(j)})$ forces a larger index. This contradiction shows that only finitely many $T(Q)$ occur.

concepts.c:algebraic-number: Algebraic coefficients let the auxiliary polynomial argument control the heights.
concepts.c:linear-subspace: The conclusion confines all solutions to finitely many proper subspaces.
concepts.c:convex-body: Each solution lies in a thin convex body to which Minkowski's theorem applies.

source.ref: W. M. Schmidt, Diophantine Approximation, Lecture Notes in Mathematics 785, Springer, 1980, Chapter V; the original is W. M. Schmidt, Norm form equations, Annals of Mathematics 96 (1972), 526-551; a modern complete proof is in E. Bombieri and W. Gubler, Heights in Diophantine Geometry, Cambridge University Press, 2006, Chapter 7.
source.note: Schmidt's proof combines Minkowski's second theorem with Roth's method of auxiliary polynomials; Bombieri and Gubler give a full proof for number fields.

statement: Let $(\Lambda V,d)$ be a minimal Sullivan algebra over $\mathbb{Q}$ with $V=V^{\ge2}$ of finite type. The simplicial set $\langle\Lambda V\rangle_n=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathrm{CDGA}}(\Lambda V,A_{PL}(\Delta^n))$ is a simply connected [Kan complex](c:kan-complex) with $\pi_n\cong\operatorname{Hom}(V^n,\mathbb{Q})$ for $n\ge2$, and $\Lambda V\to A_{PL}(\langle\Lambda V\rangle)$ is a [quasi-isomorphism](c:quasi-isomorphism).

hypotheses.text: $(\Lambda V,d)$ is a commutative [dg-algebra](c:dg-algebra-2) over $\mathbb{Q}$, free on a graded space $V$, with $d(V)\subseteq\Lambda^{\ge2}V$.
The space $V$ is concentrated in degrees $\ge2$, so the realization is simply connected.
Each graded piece $V^n$ is finite dimensional.

conclusion: The realization $\langle\Lambda V\rangle$ is a simply connected [Kan complex](c:kan-complex) of finite type with rational homotopy groups $\operatorname{Hom}(V^n,\mathbb{Q})$ and Sullivan model $\Lambda V$.

proofs.name: Realization adjoint to polynomial forms
proofs.slogan: Realize the algebra through polynomial forms on simplices, show that the result is Kan, read off its homotopy groups, and compare the algebra with the forms of the realization.
proofs.scope: This is an outline of the Bousfield-Gugenheim proof for minimal Sullivan algebras; the steps that rest on the cited work are marked. A general commutative dg-algebra reduces to this case through its minimal Sullivan model, and the Sullivan construction on all of them is the family.

roles.why: Freeness of $\Lambda V$ gives the lifting property that makes the realization Kan and lets homotopy classes be computed.
Degrees $\ge2$ for $V$ make the realization connected and simply connected.
Finite type makes the tower of principal fibrations converge and the groups finite dimensional.

steps.slogan: Define the realization and its adjunction with polynomial forms.
steps.detail: Set $\langle A\rangle_n=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathrm{CDGA}}(A,A_{PL}(\Delta^n))$ with faces and degeneracies from $\Delta^\bullet$. Because $A_{PL}(K)=\operatorname{Hom}_{sSet}(K,A_{PL}^\bullet)$, there is a natural bijection $\operatorname{Hom}_{sSet}(K,\langle A\rangle)\cong\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathrm{CDGA}}(A,A_{PL}(K))$.

steps.slogan: Show that the realization of a Sullivan algebra is a Kan complex.
steps.detail: A horn $\Lambda^n_k\to\langle\Lambda V\rangle$ is an algebra map $\Lambda V\to A_{PL}(\Lambda^n_k)$. The restriction $A_{PL}(\Delta^n)\to A_{PL}(\Lambda^n_k)$ is onto and a quasi-isomorphism by the PL de Rham theorem. A Sullivan algebra lifts along such maps by induction on generators, so the horn fills.

steps.slogan: Compute the homotopy groups from homotopy classes of maps to a model of the sphere.
steps.detail: The group $\pi_n\langle\Lambda V\rangle$ is the set of homotopy classes of maps $\Lambda V\to A_{PL}(S^n)\simeq\mathbb{Q}\oplus\mathbb{Q}x_n$. For a minimal algebra such a map kills decomposables and every $V^k$ with $k\ne n$, so the classes correspond to $\operatorname{Hom}(V^n,\mathbb{Q})$. This step rests on the cited work.

steps.slogan: Prove that the adjunction map is a quasi-isomorphism by induction on degree.
steps.detail: Filter $\Lambda V$ by the subalgebras generated by $V^{\le n}$. The realizations form a tower of principal fibrations with fibres $K(\operatorname{Hom}(V^n,\mathbb{Q}),n)$. Comparing Serre spectral sequences, with finite type controlling the limit, shows that $\Lambda V\to A_{PL}(\langle\Lambda V\rangle)$ is a [quasi-isomorphism](c:quasi-isomorphism). This step rests on the cited work.

steps.slogan: Collect the properties of the realization.
steps.detail: By step 2 the realization is a [Kan complex](c:kan-complex). Step 3 and $V^1=0$ show that it is simply connected with $\pi_n\cong\operatorname{Hom}(V^n,\mathbb{Q})$, a finite dimensional rational vector space. Step 4 shows that $\Lambda V$ is its Sullivan model.

concepts.c:kan-complex: Kan fillers make homotopy groups and the lifting arguments available.
concepts.c:quasi-isomorphism: Quasi-isomorphisms are the maps between algebras that the realization respects.
concepts.c:dg-algebra-2: The input is a commutative dg-algebra built freely on a graded space.

source.ref: A. K. Bousfield and V. K. A. M. Gugenheim, On PL de Rham theory and rational homotopy type, Memoirs of the American Mathematical Society 8, no. 179 (1976); see also Y. Félix, S. Halperin and J.-C. Thomas, Rational Homotopy Theory, Graduate Texts in Mathematics 205, Springer, 2001, Section 17.
source.note: Bousfield and Gugenheim prove the adjunction between polynomial forms and realization; Felix, Halperin and Thomas give the spatial realization of Sullivan algebras.

statement: Let $K$ be a [number field](c:number-field), $\mathfrak{m}$ a modulus, and $H$ a subgroup of the group $I^{\mathfrak{m}}$ of ideals prime to $\mathfrak{m}$ that contains the ray $P_{\mathfrak{m}}$. Then there is a unique finite [abelian extension](c:abelian-extension) $L/K$ unramified outside $\mathfrak{m}$ whose [Artin map](c:artin-map) $I^{\mathfrak{m}}\to\operatorname{Gal}(L/K)$ is onto with kernel $H$.

hypotheses.text: $K$ is a [number field](c:number-field) and $\mathfrak{m}$ is a modulus of $K$.
$H$ is a subgroup of $I^{\mathfrak{m}}$ containing the ray $P_{\mathfrak{m}}$, so $I^{\mathfrak{m}}/H$ is a quotient of the [ray class group](c:ray-class-group).

conclusion: Some finite abelian extension $L/K$ has $I^{\mathfrak{m}}/H\cong\operatorname{Gal}(L/K)$ by the Artin map, and it is the only one; so abelian extensions and congruence subgroups correspond with inclusion reversed.

proofs.name: Kummer theory and descent
proofs.slogan: Attach norm groups through Artin reciprocity, show that they determine the extension, then construct the extension for exponent $n$ by Kummer theory and descend to $K$.
proofs.scope: This is an outline of Takagi's proof for number fields, with the steps that rest on the cited work marked. The idelic form for global fields and the version with infinite places are other members of the family.

roles.why: Number fields have the unit theorem, finite class numbers and the Artin map that the proof uses.
The quotient $I^{\mathfrak{m}}/H$ is finite, so some exponent $n$ kills it, and $H\supseteq P_{\mathfrak{m}}$ makes it a congruence subgroup.

steps.slogan: Attach a norm group to each abelian extension through the Artin map.
steps.detail: For a finite abelian $L/K$ and a modulus $\mathfrak{m}$ divisible by the conductor, Artin reciprocity says that the [Artin map](c:artin-map) $I^{\mathfrak{m}}\to\operatorname{Gal}(L/K)$ is onto with kernel $H_L=P_{\mathfrak{m}}N_{L/K}(I_L^{\mathfrak{m}})$. So $H_L$ is a congruence subgroup.

steps.slogan: Show that a norm group determines the extension.
steps.detail: By the Chebotarev density theorem, a finite Galois extension is determined by the set of primes that split completely in it. A prime $\mathfrak{p}\nmid\mathfrak{m}$ splits completely in $L$ exactly when $\mathfrak{p}\in H_L$. So $L\mapsto H_L$ is injective and reverses inclusion; this proves uniqueness.

steps.slogan: Reduce existence to an abelian extension of exponent $n$ over a field with $n$-th roots of unity.
steps.detail: The group $I^{\mathfrak{m}}/H$ is finite, so $n$ kills it. Put $K'=K(\zeta_n)$. By Kummer theory the abelian extensions of $K'$ of exponent dividing $n$ are the subextensions of $K'(\sqrt[n]{a})$ for $a\in K'^{\times}$, so existence over $K'$ becomes a question about $n$-th power classes.

steps.slogan: Construct the extension of $K'$ with the prescribed norm group by Kummer theory and counting.
steps.detail: Takagi compares the degree of the maximal Kummer extension with conductor dividing a given modulus with the index of $P_{\mathfrak{m}'}I'^{\,n}$ in $I'^{\mathfrak{m}'}$. The unit theorem, finiteness of the class number and the first and second inequalities give equality, so the extension has norm group exactly $P_{\mathfrak{m}'}I'^{\,n}$. This step rests on the cited work.

steps.slogan: Descend from $K'$ to $K$ and read off the class field of $H$.
steps.detail: The norm group $N_{K'/K}^{-1}(H)$ is stable under $\operatorname{Gal}(K'/K)$, so its class field $L'$ is Galois over $K$. Comparing norm indices through the reciprocity law yields a subextension $L/K$, abelian over $K$, with $H_L=H$. This step rests on the cited work.

steps.slogan: Combine existence and uniqueness into the correspondence.
steps.detail: Step 5 gives an abelian $L/K$ with Artin kernel $H$, and step 2 shows that it is unique. So $H\mapsto L$ and $L\mapsto H_L$ are inverse, inclusion-reversing bijections for a fixed modulus.

concepts.c:number-field: The unit theorem and class number finiteness hold for number fields.
concepts.c:ray-class-group: Its quotients are the generalized ideal class groups of the theorem.
concepts.c:abelian-extension: These extensions are the objects that the groups $H$ classify.
concepts.c:artin-map: The Artin map identifies the quotient $I^{\mathfrak{m}}/H$ with the Galois group.

statement: Let $G$ be a [compact group](c:compact-group). Let $h=(h_V)_V$ be a family of unitary operators on the finite-dimensional unitary [representations](c:unitary-representation) $V$ of $G$ that commutes with every intertwiner and satisfies $h_{V\otimes W}=h_V\otimes h_W$. Then $h=(\pi_V(x))_V$ for exactly one $x\in G$.

hypotheses.text: $G$ is a [compact group](c:compact-group), Hausdorff as a topological space.
The family $(h_V)_V$ is a tensor automorphism of the forgetful [fiber functor](c:fiber-functor) on the [representation category](c:representation-category) of $G$.

conclusion: The map $x\mapsto(\pi_V(x))_V$ is a bijection, and a homeomorphism, from $G$ onto the group of tensor automorphisms of the forgetful functor.

proofs.name: Peter-Weyl density argument
proofs.slogan:
Tensor automorphisms form a compact group $H\supseteq G$; a Peter-Weyl argument excludes $G
e H$ through a nontrivial representation with an $H$-fixed vector.
proofs.scope: All compact Hausdorff groups, including finite ones. Naturality is required for all intertwiners, so it applies to subrepresentations and not only to irreducible pieces.

roles.why: Compactness gives Haar measure, Peter-Weyl, and the closedness of the image of $G$.
Naturality and monoidality define the group $H$, turn its elements into operators, and fix invariant vectors.

steps.slogan: Form the group $H$ of tensor automorphisms and the map $\iota\colon G\to H$.
steps.detail: The group $H$ is a closed subgroup of $\prod_VU(V)$, so it is a compact Hausdorff group, and each $V$ is a unitary $H$-representation by $k\mapsto k_V$. The trivial representation $\mathbb{1}$ has $k_{\mathbb{1}}=1$, because $k_{\mathbb{1}}=k_{\mathbb{1}}\otimes k_{\mathbb{1}}$. The map $\iota(x)=(\pi_V(x))_V$ is a continuous homomorphism.

steps.slogan: Show that $\iota$ is injective with closed image by the Peter-Weyl theorem.
steps.detail: By the Peter-Weyl theorem the matrix coefficients of finite-dimensional unitary representations separate the points of $G$. If $\iota(x)=\iota(y)$, all coefficients agree at $x$ and $y$, so $x=y$. A continuous injection from a compact space into a Hausdorff space is a homeomorphism onto a closed subgroup.

steps.slogan: Show that a vector of $V$ fixed by $G$ is fixed by all of $H$.
steps.detail: Let $u\in V$ satisfy $\pi_V(x)u=u$ for all $x$. The line $\mathbb{C}u$ is a subrepresentation isomorphic to $\mathbb{1}$, so its inclusion is an intertwiner. Naturality gives $k_Vu=k_{\mathbb{1}}u=u$ for every $k\in H$.

steps.slogan: Show that every irreducible representation of $H$ occurs inside some $V$.
steps.detail: The functions $k\mapsto\langle k_Vv,w\rangle$ separate points of $H$, contain constants, and are closed under products (monoidality) and conjugation ($h_{\bar V}=\overline{h_V}$, by step 3 on the invariant vector of $V\otimes\bar V$). So they are dense by Stone-Weierstrass. They span a bi-translation invariant space, so it contains the coefficients of every irreducible $H$-representation $W$; hence $W\subseteq V$ for some $V$.

steps.slogan: Conclude that $\iota$ is onto by contradiction.
steps.detail: Suppose $\iota(G)\ne H$. A nonconstant continuous function on the compact space $H/\iota(G)$, pulled back to $H$, has a nonzero component in the coefficients of a nontrivial irreducible $H$-representation $W$ with a nonzero $\iota(G)$-fixed vector (use the dual if needed). Step 4 puts $W$ inside some $V$, and step 3 makes the vector $H$-fixed. Then $W$ is trivial, a contradiction.

concepts.c:compact-group: Compactness gives Peter-Weyl, Haar measure and a closed image of $G$.
concepts.c:unitary-representation: The operators $h_V$ act on finite-dimensional unitary representations.
concepts.c:fiber-functor: The forgetful functor is the fiber functor whose tensor automorphisms form $H$.
concepts.c:representation-category: Intertwiners and tensor products of this category define naturality and monoidality.

source.note: A direct Peter-Weyl proof of the narrow Tannaka-Krein theorem for compact groups; the original results are T. Tannaka, Tohoku Math. J. 45 (1939), 1-12, and M. G. Krein, Dokl. Akad. Nauk SSSR 69 (1949), 725-728.
